analysis.one_liner: Gives auto makers a doubled tax deduction for worker wages while repealing car and truck pollution and fuel-economy rules.
analysis.headline: The bill has sat in the Senate Finance Committee since its introduction in February 2025, with no committee action, floor vote, or additional cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would let U.S. auto manufacturers deduct twice the wages they pay assembly workers, provided the company makes at least 75% of its vehicles and key parts in the U.S. and provides platinum-level health coverage, pensions, and profit-sharing. At the same time, it would erase the 2024 EPA and highway-safety rules that cut car and truck pollution and raise fuel economy, strip California and other states of their power to set stricter standards, and require replacement standards that cannot push companies toward electric vehicles. The tax break and the deregulation both lower the auto industry's costs.
analysis.who_benefits: Domestic auto manufacturers gain the most: a deduction worth up to twice their eligible wage costs (capped at $150,000 per worker), a reduction in the income their alternative minimum tax is computed on, and the end of compliance obligations under the 2024 emissions and fuel-economy rules. Gasoline producers gain from weaker fuel-economy standards, which mean more fuel burned per mile. Nonunion plants also gain because the deduction requires companies to stay neutral in union organizing drives rather than support them.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Domestic auto makers and gasoline producers

how_it_helps.text: Auto manufacturers can deduct 200% of eligible wages paid to U.S. auto and parts workers, if at least 75% of their vehicles, engines, transmissions, and battery cells for U.S. sale are made in the U.S. and they did not move production offshore the prior year [S3].
Companies can subtract the same wages from the financial-statement income used to calculate the corporate alternative minimum tax, cutting that liability further [S3].

The bill nullifies the EPA's 2024 light- and medium-duty vehicle emissions rule, the Phase 3 heavy-duty truck rule, and NHTSA's 2027-and-later fuel economy rules, removing the compliance costs attached to them [S3].

It revokes every existing Clean Air Act waiver, including California's zero-emission vehicle mandate, repeals the provision letting other states adopt California's rules, and bars any future state-specific standards [S3].

Replacement standards written under the bill must be 'economically practicable' and may not directly or indirectly require the production or sale of electric vehicles, and compliance with either standard counts as compliance with the other [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Drivers pay more at the pump because the fuel-economy rules that reduce gasoline consumption per mile are erased, and the replacement standards cannot require more efficient electric vehicles. The public bears higher tailpipe pollution and its health costs, since the repealed rules set the emission limits for cars and trucks through the 2030s. States lose the authority they currently have to set stricter vehicle standards than the federal government, and the EPA and NHTSA lose rules they spent years writing.

drawbacks.text: Repealing the 2024 fuel-economy and emissions standards leaves cars and trucks burning more gasoline and emitting more pollution than they would under the rules, and the bill forbids the replacement standards from pushing the market toward electric vehicles [S3].

The doubled wage deduction costs the Treasury up to 42 cents for every deductible wage dollar at the 21% corporate rate, and it applies only to wages up to $150,000 per worker, concentrating the benefit at large manufacturers rather than small shops [S3].

The bill's wage deduction is conditioned on platinum-level health coverage and pension promises of 50% wage replacement, terms most nonunion plants do not currently meet, so the tax break may reach mainly the largest unionized-adjacent manufacturers even as it requires only union 'neutrality' [S3].
Revoking all existing Clean Air Act waivers overrides the standards that California and more than a dozen states have adopted to cut local air pollution [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The wage deduction is the one provision that could plausibly help ordinary autoworkers, since the tax break only arrives if companies pay above the 75th percentile of wages in the industry and offer strong health and retirement benefits. But it is paired with a broad rollback of pollution and fuel-economy rules whose main effect is to lower manufacturers' compliance costs while raising consumers' gasoline bills and public health costs. On balance, the bill transfers far more to the industry than it returns to the public.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in the Senate and referred to the Finance Committee, where it has sat without a hearing, amendment, or vote since February 2025.

narrative.text: Senator Bernie Moreno introduced the Transportation Freedom Act on February 25, 2025, joined by Senators Sheehy, Banks, and Justice as cosponsors [S1].
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance, and the action history shows no further steps [S5].
The bill has three cosponsors, all Republicans, out of 55 Senate Republicans [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Nothing has happened yet, so the current rules remain in force: drivers still benefit from the 2024 fuel-economy and emissions standards, and the auto industry still bears the compliance costs the bill would erase. If the bill stays in committee, it will be the manufacturers and gasoline producers who are spared the tighter standards, not through a vote but through inaction.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: So far, no one; the current rules stand

sides.party_line_note: All four backers are Republicans (3 of 55 Senate Republicans as cosponsors), no Democrat or Independent has cosponsored, and no floor action has been taken.

industries.note: The bill hands manufacturers a doubled wage deduction, cuts their minimum tax base, and erases the 2024 emissions and fuel-economy rules. The wage deduction comes with real worker-protection conditions, but the deregulation lowers their costs while drivers pay more at the pump.

Weaker fuel-economy standards mean more gasoline burned per mile for decades, increasing demand for their product at drivers' expense. The ban on standards that favor electric vehicles protects that market position.

The bill nullifies the emissions rules and the California zero-emission vehicle mandate that drove EV demand, and forbids new standards from requiring electric vehicles, cutting the policy floor out from under the EV market.

industries.industry: State governments (California and states adopting its standards)
industries.note: The bill revokes all existing Clean Air Act waivers and repeals the provision letting states adopt California's standards, removing their ability to cut local air pollution beyond federal minimums.

analysis.trajectory: The bill sits in the Senate Finance Committee with three cosponsors and no action in months. Bills of this kind rarely move without a committee hearing or bipartisan support, so the most likely path is that it remains in committee and dies when the Congress ends.
